inline.s: If I attain Buddhahood, may the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their own vows, whatever Dharma they wish to hear, hear it spontaneously. If it be not so, may I not attain right enlightenment.
(Vow 46: Hearing the Dharma as Vowed)
If I attain Buddhahood, may the hosts of bodhisattvas in other lands, upon hearing my name, at once attain non-regression. If it be not so, may I not attain right enlightenment.
(Vow 47: Non-Regression on Hearing the Name)

If I attain Buddhahood, may the hosts of bodhisattvas in other lands, upon hearing my name, at once attain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and in the Buddha-Dharma immediately attain non-regression. If it be not so, may I not attain right enlightenment.
(Vow 48: Attaining the Three Patient Acceptances)
The Buddha told Ananda: At that time, after the Bhiksu Dharmakara had proclaimed these vows, he uttered a verse:
I set a resolve surpassing the world to reach the supreme Way; if these vows remain unfilled, I vow never to attain enlightenment.
Again I make myself a great donor, giving relief to all in poverty and distress, that all these hosts of beings may know no sorrow or trouble through the long night.
I give rise to all roots of good and accomplish the fruit of bodhi; if I attain enlightenment, I shall take the name of Immeasurable Life.
Beings hearing this name will all come to my land, with bodies of gold like the Buddha’s, their subtle marks all perfectly complete.
With a heart of great compassion, I shall benefit all the many beings, and, detached from desire, in deep right mindfulness, with pure wisdom, cultivate the pure conduct.
May my wisdom-light universally shine upon the lands of the ten directions, dispelling the darkness of the three defilements, and clearly saving beings from all calamities.
All beings shall relinquish the suffering of the three evil paths, extinguishing the darkness of all afflictions, opening the eye of wisdom and attaining a body of light.
I shall close off every evil path and open the gate to the realms of good; for beings I shall open the treasury of Dharma and widely bestow the jewels of merit.
Like the Buddha’s unobstructed wisdom, I shall practice the conduct of compassion; I shall always be the teacher of gods and humans, and become the hero of the three realms.
I shall expound the Dharma with a lion’s roar, widely crossing over all sentient beings, fulfilling the vows made in the past, that all may become Buddhas.
If these vows are accomplished, the great thousand worlds shall be moved; the gods of the sky shall rain down wondrous and precious flowers.

The Buddha told Ananda: After the Bhiksu Dharmakara had spoken this verse, at once the whole earth moved in six ways. Heaven rained wondrous flowers, scattering them over him; and spontaneously celestial music arose, while a voice in the sky proclaimed: “You shall surely attain supreme right enlightenment.”

Ananda, after the Bhiksu Dharmakara had proclaimed these great vows before the Tathagata Lokesvararaja and amidst the assemblies of gods and humans, he abode in true wisdom, vigorously and earnestly advanced, and with single mind devoted himself to adorning that wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was vast and broad, surpassing and uniquely wonderful, established eternal, without decline or change.

For immeasurable kalpas he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, anger, delusion, or desire; he was not attached to sights, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangible objects. He delighted only in recollecting the roots of good cultivated by all the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the tranquil conduct, far from all falsehood. Relying upon the gate of true reality, he planted the roots of all virtue, mindful not of the many sufferings.

With few desires and content, he sought only the wholesome Dharma to benefit beings. His vows never tired, and his power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he constantly harbored compassion and forbearance. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he exhorted and encouraged them. He honored the Three Jewels and served teachers and elders, without any false or flattering mind.

He adorned all his conduct, and was complete in all standards of deportment. He contemplated all dharmas as illusion, and his samadhi was ever still. He well guarded his speech-karma, never ridiculing the faults of others; he well guarded his body-karma, never failing in the rules of conduct; he well guarded his mind-karma, pure and undefiled. All cities, villages, relatives, and precious treasures he held entirely without attachment. Always by the six perfections of giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, he taught and established sentient beings to abide in the supreme, true Way.

Because of the accomplishment of such roots of good, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures spontaneously arose and responded. Sometimes he was a householder or a wealthy elder, of noble lineage and high rank; sometimes a noble warrior, a king, or a wheel-turning sage-king; sometimes the lord of the sixth desire heaven, up to the Brahma king. At the abodes of all Buddhas he paid respect and made offerings, without ever a break. Such merits cannot be fully told.
From his body and mouth there constantly issued immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like
(zhān)

sandalwood and utpala flowers, whose fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his appearance and marks were dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty minor marks were all complete. From his hands there constantly issued inexhaustible treasures and ornaments of adornment, the supreme articles for all needs, benefiting and delighting sentient beings. By these causes, he could cause immeasurable beings all to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

The Buddha told Ananda: The Bhiksu Dharmakara, cultivating the bodhisattva path, accumulated merit and virtue immeasurably, boundlessly. In all dharmas he attained mastery, beyond the comprehension of speech and discrimination. The vows he had made were fully accomplished; he truly abode, complete in adornment, in a Buddha-land vast in majestic virtue and pure.

Ananda, hearing what the Buddha said, addressed the World-Honored One: “The bodhisattva Dharmakara who attained bodhi—is he a Buddha of the past, or of the future? Or is he now present in another world?”

The World-Honored One answered: “That Tathagata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; he is unborn and unceasing, not in the past, present, or future. Only because he fulfills his vows to save beings, he is now in the West, a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands away, in a world named the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Dharmakara became a Buddha, named Amitabha. Since he attained Buddhahood, now ten kalpas have passed. Now he is present and speaks the Dharma, with an assembly of immeasurable, countless bodhisattvas and sravakas respectfully surrounding him.”

blocks.text: 10. All Making the Vow to Become a Buddha

inline.s: The Buddha spoke of how Amitabha Buddha, as a bodhisattva, obtained these vows. At that time the crown prince Ajatasatru and five hundred sons of elders, hearing it, all greatly rejoiced. Each took a golden flower-canopy, and together they came before the Buddha and paid homage. Having offered the canopies upon the Buddha, they withdrew and sat in a place apart to listen to the sutra, and in their hearts made the wish: “May we, when we become Buddhas, be just like Amitabha Buddha.”

The Buddha, knowing this, told the monks: “This prince and the others shall in the future become Buddhas. In past lives they dwelt on the bodhisattva path and, through countless kalpas, made offerings to forty kotis of Buddhas. In the time of Kasyapa Buddha they were my disciples; now they make offerings to me, and we meet again.” At that the monks, hearing the Buddha’s words, all rejoiced on their behalf.

The Buddha said to Ananda: “In that Land of Ultimate Bliss, immeasurable merits are fully adorned. There is forever no name of the many sufferings, calamities, evil destinies, or mara afflictions. Nor is there any difference of the four seasons, cold or heat, or rain and gloom. It is peaceful and harmonious, blissful beyond compare.”

Its ground has no sea, but has rivers. There are no hills, pits, thorns, gravel, or mountains of iron, Sumeru, or earth and stone. Only from the natural seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, conch
(chē qú)
, and agate—is the ground formed, broad and level, without limit. Subtle and marvelously lovely, pure and adorned, it surpasses all the worlds of the ten directions.”
Ananda, having heard this, addressed the World-Honored One: “If that land has no Mount Sumeru, upon what do the four heavenly kings and the Trayastrimsa heaven rely?”
The Buddha told Ananda: “The Yama, Tusita, and up to the form and formless realms, the heavens—upon what do they rely?”
Ananda replied: “It is due to inconceivable karmic power.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “This inconceivable karma—can you know it? The retribution of your own body is inconceivable; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is also inconceivable; the good roots of sentient beings are inconceivable; the sacred power of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable. The beings of that land, through the power of merit and virtue, abide in the stage of karma, and by the Buddha’s spiritual power, are able to be thus.”

Ananda replied: “Karmic cause and retribution are inconceivable! In this teaching I am truly without doubt. Only for the sake of future beings, to break through the net of doubt, do I raise this question.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Amitabha Buddha’s majestic light is supremely honored, first of all, beyond the reach of all the Buddhas of the ten directions. It universally illuminates the Buddha-lands of the East, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and so too the South, the West, the North, the four intermediate quarters, above and below. The lights of the Buddhas may illuminate one or two Buddha-lands, or a hundred or a thousand. Only Amitabha Buddha’s light universally shines upon immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.”

As to how far or near the lights of the Buddhas shine, this was determined by the vows and merits they made when seeking the Way as bodhisattvas, whether great or small. When they became Buddhas, each obtained what he had sought.

Amitabha Buddha’s light is excellent and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon by a thousand kotis of times. It is the most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas. Therefore Amitabha Buddha is also named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, also the Buddha of Boundless Light, of Unobstructed Light, of Incomparable Light; also the Light of Wisdom, the Light of Constantly Shining, the Light of Purity, the Light of Joy, the Light of Liberation, the Light of Peace, the Light Surpassing Sun and Moon, and the Light of Inconceivable.

Such light universally illuminates all the worlds in the ten directions. Beings who encounter this light have their defilements extinguished and their goodness increased; their bodies and minds become gentle. If they are in the three evil paths in places of extreme suffering, seeing this light they all gain rest, and at the end of life all attain liberation. If beings hear of this light’s majestic power and merit, and speak of it day and night with single-mindedness and without interruption, according to their wishes they shall be born in that land.

The Buddha said to Ananda: “Amitabha Buddha’s lifespan is long and enduring, immeasurable. The host of bodhisattvas, sravakas, gods, and humans—their lifespan and number are likewise beyond the reach of calculation and simile.”

“Among my disciples, Mahamaudgalyayana is foremost in supernormal powers. In the three-thousand great-thousand world, all the stars and beings, in a single day and night, he knows their number. Suppose all beings in the ten directions became pratyekabuddhas, each with a lifespan of a kotis of years, each with supernormal powers like Mahamaudgalyayana. Exhausting their lives and all their intellect to calculate the measure together, of a hundred parts they would not know one; of a thousand parts, a hundred thousand parts, and even in the
(wū)
upanishada portions, they would not know one.”

“It is like the great ocean, deep and broad without bound. Suppose one took a single hair and split it into a hundred parts; with one of those parts one takes a drop of water from the ocean. Between this single drop and the ocean, which is the more? Ananda, what Mahamaudgalyayana and the rest can know is like such a drop; what they cannot know is like the water of the ocean. Amitabha Buddha’s lifespan, and the lifespan and number of the people of that land, are likewise, beyond the reach of calculation and simile.”

blocks.text: 14. Flowers and Trees Throughout the Land

inline.s: Moreover, Ananda, in that Land of Ultimate Bliss, immeasurable merits are fully adorned. All sorts of wondrous flowers likewise fill it, everywhere pervaded with fragrance
(fù)
. There are seven-jeweled banners set in rows. Upon these jeweled banners hang streamers and canopies and many jeweled bells, replete with a hundred thousand subtle and varied colors.
Ananda, in that Tathagata’s land there are

many jeweled trees. Some are pure gold trees, pure silver trees, pure lapis trees, pure coral trees, pure amber trees, pure conch trees, pure agate trees, each formed solely of one treasure, not mixed with other treasures. Or there are trees of two or three treasures, up to seven treasures, made by combining them. Their trunks, stems, branches, and roots are formed of these treasures; their flowers, leaves, and fruits are transformed from other treasures, all various and combined.
Each row is separate; row faces row, stem watches stem, branch and leaf reach toward one another, flower and fruit correspond; their hues blaze with brilliance, too much to behold.
A net of seven treasures spreads over them, soft as katapas cotton.
A clear breeze at times rises, producing five sounds, subtle as the notes of the scale, naturally harmonized. These jeweled trees fill the whole land
, their radiance resplendent, nothing in the world can compare.”

At its enlightenment-seat there is a bodhi-tree, four million li high. Its trunk is five thousand yojanas around; its branches and leaves spread, twenty thousand li. All precious treasures spontaneously formed it. Flowers and fruits bloom in profusion, their light shining everywhere. There are also red, green, blue, and white manis, the king of treasures, serving as its garlands. Cloud-gathered jeweled chains adorn its jeweled pillars. Golden bells and chimes
(duó)
hang throughout its branches.”

“A precious, wondrous net is spread over it. A hundred thousand myriad colors adorn one another; immeasurable light and radiance shine without end; all its adornments appear as fitting. A gentle breeze moves, blowing its branches and leaves, drawing forth immeasurable sounds of the wondrous Dharma. The sound flows and spreads to all Buddha-lands. Pure and clear, poignant and brilliant, subtle and harmonious—among the sounds of the ten directions it is foremost.”

“If beings look upon the bodhi-tree, hear its sound, smell its fragrance, taste the flavor of its fruit, touch its light and shadow, or recollect its merits, they shall all attain the six faculties pure and clear, without afflictions, abiding in non-regression until they reach the Buddha Way. Moreover, by seeing that tree, they obtain three kinds of patient acceptance: first, acceptance of sounds; second, acceptance of compliance; third, acceptance of the unproduced Dharma.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “In such a Buddha-land, flowers, fruits, and trees work as Buddha-work for the many beings. All this is through Amitabha Buddha’s majestic power, his primal vow-power, his power of fulfilled vows, and his clear, firm, and ultimate vow-power.”
Moreover, the lecture halls and residences, the towers
guàn

and railings, are likewise all formed spontaneously of the seven treasures; there are also white pearls and mani gems strung in network, exceedingly luminous and wondrous. The palaces where the bodhisattvas dwell are likewise so.

Some there are on the ground explaining the sutra or reciting it; some receiving it and listening to it; some walking in meditation on the ground, contemplating the Way and sitting in meditation; some in the sky explaining, reciting, receiving, and listening; some walking in meditation, contemplating the Way, and sitting in meditation.

Some attain srotaapanna, some sakrdagamin, some anagamin, or arhatship. Those who have not attained the irreversibility do attain it. Each reflects on the Way, speaks of the Way, and practices the Way, all not without joy.

The Buddha told Ananda: “In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there is no sea but there are rivers, crisscrossing in every direction, with golden sand spread over their beds. In width they are perhaps ten yojanas, twenty, or thirty yojanas, up to a hundred thousand yojanas, and twelve yojanas deep.”

“The water is calm, fragrant, and clean, tasting like ambrosia, endowed with eight qualities: first, clear; second, cool; third, sweet; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, peaceful and harmonious; seventh, when drunk it removes hunger, thirst, and countless other ills; eighth, when drunk it is certain to nourish the faculties and the four great elements, increasing all manner of supreme and excellent roots of good.”

“There are famous flowers floating down with the stream. A gentle breeze stirring, all sorts of fragrance are produced. On both banks grow sandalwood trees, heavenly mandarava flowers, utpala flowers,
padma flowers, kumuda flowers

, and pundarika flowers; their long branches and dense leaves intertwine over the river, blooming and bearing fruit, their fragrant brilliance a delight. Hosts of beings sport and play, coming and going as they please. Some wade into the river to bathe
(zhuó)
and romp. Deep or shallow, cold or warm, all conform to people’s wishes. There are heavenly fragrances that scatter their scent with the wind
(fù)

“The lecture halls and residences, and the dwellings where the bodhisattvas and arhats live, have bathing pools within and without, on all sides; either ten yojanas, or twenty, thirty, up to a hundred thousand yojanas, equal in length and breadth. The golden pool has silver sand at its bottom; the silver pool, golden sand; the crystal pool, lapis sand; the lapis pool, crystal sand; the coral pool, amber sand; the amber pool, coral sand; the conch pool, agate sand; the agate pool, conch sand; the white jade pool, purple-gold sand; the purple-gold pool, white-jade sand. On the shores grow sandalwood trees, their flowers and leaves hanging and spreading, their fragrance pervasively diffused. The water of the eight qualities fills them. When one wishes to bathe, he enters the pool and bathes. If he wishes the water to reach his feet, his knees, his waist, his armpits, or his neck; or wishes to pour it over his body; or wishes it cold, warm, swift, or slow—the water follows every wish, opening the spirit and delighting the body.”

“Amitabha Buddha’s jeweled pool is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. The natural seven treasures are combined to form it. The sand at its bottom is all white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani gems. The water of the eight qualities is pure as if without form; gems and sand shine through it, and there is no depth it does not illume. Gentle ripples slowly turn, pouring into one another. On its shores are sandalwood trees, auspicious fruit trees
, heavenly mandarava flowers

, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kunuda flowers, and pundarika flowers—fresh flowers and great fruit, ever blooming in splendor, their light shining, of utmost beauty. Long branches and dense leaves interweave over the water. All sorts of fragrance are produced, beyond all comparison, and the perfume drifts along the stream.”

“The waves raise immeasurable, subtle sounds; one hears the sound of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; the sound of the perfections; the sound of stilling and quiescence; the sound of the unborn and unceasing; the sound of the ten powers and the fearlessnesses; or the sound of no self-nature, no fabrication, no self; the sound of great compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and giving; the sound of ambrosia sprinkling the crown and receiving the prediction. Having heard such manifold sounds, the mind becomes pure and without discriminations, upright and equal, ripening all roots of good. Whatever one hears accords with the Dharma. Those who wish to hear, hear it alone
(zhé)
; what they do not wish to hear, they hear nothing of it. Never do they regress from the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
In that Land of Ultimate Bliss,
the bodhisattvas, sravakas, gods, and humans, with wisdom lofty and clear, supernormal powers thorough and penetrating, are all of one kind,
free of any distinguishing marks.
Their countenances upright, their forms and colors subtle, surpassing and rare in the world, neither gods nor humans, they all receive a naturally pure and ethereal body, a body without limit.

The Buddha told Ananda: “Consider the poor beggars of the world: standing beside a king, could their faces and forms be compared? If a king were compared to a wheel-turning sage-king, he would be base and ugly, just as that beggar beside the king. The wheel-turning sage-king, foremost in majestic marks, compared to the king of Trayastrimsa heaven, would be yet more ugly and inferior. Even the king of Trayastrimsa, compared to the king of the heaven of enjoying others’ transformations, does not come close, not by a hundred thousand times. The king of the heaven of enjoying others’ transformations, compared to the bodhisattvas and sravakas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in luminous countenance and hue, does not come near them, not by a crore of times.”

The palaces they dwell in, their clothing, food, and drink, are like those of the king of the heaven of enjoying others’ transformations. As for their majestic virtue, rank, supernormal powers, and transformations, all the gods and humans cannot be compared to them, not by a hundred thousand myriads of kotis.
Ananda, you should know that the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha has such accumulated merit and adornment, inconceivable!

Moreover, all beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whether already born, now born, or to be born, all obtain such wondrous forms and bodies. Their appearance is upright and dignified, their merit and virtue immeasurable. Their wisdom is clear and bright, their supernormal powers free and spontaneous. All manner of enjoyments are entirely abundant. Palaces, clothing, ornaments, flowers, streamers, canopies, and all furnishings of adornment, whatever they desire, all appear as one wishes.

When one wishes to eat, jeweled bowls of the seven treasures spontaneously appear before him, and the hundred flavors of food spontaneously fill them. Though there is this food, in truth there is none who eats it. Only seeing its colors and smelling its fragrance, one is nourished by thought; strength and vitality increase, without any waste. The body and mind become gentle and soft, without attachment to any taste. When the meal is over it vanishes, and in due time appears again.
There are also superb garments of many treasures, crowns, sashes, necklaces, with immeasurable light and a hundred thousand subtle colors, all complete and spontaneously upon the body.

The dwellings they dwell in have forms and colors to delight the heart. A jeweled net is spread over them, and jeweled bells are hung. Wondrous and marvelously rare, adorned all about, their brilliance dazzling, utterly majestic and beautiful. Towers, railings, halls, and chambers, broad or narrow, square or round, great or small, some in the sky, some on the ground, all pure, peaceful, and still, subtle and blissful. They appear before the mind’s call, none lacking.

“In that Buddha-land, at every mealtime, a natural virtuous wind gently and joyfully rises, blowing the jeweled nets and the many jeweled trees, producing subtle sounds that expound suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no-self, and the many perfections, and spreading abroad ten thousand kinds of gentle, elegant virtue-fragrance. Those who hear it find their dusty defilements and habitual stains naturally cease. The wind touching their bodies makes them peaceful and harmonious, like a monk who has attained the cessation samadhi.”

“It moreover blows the seven-jeweled groves and trees, sending the wafting flowers into heaps, with all sorts of colors and lights filling the Buddha-land. In order of color they are laid without confusion, soft and bright, like katapas cotton. When one sets foot upon them, the foot sinks to four fingers’ depth, and as the foot lifts they rise back to their former state. After the mealtime the flowers vanish of themselves, and the great earth is pure. In due seasons it rains new flowers, again covering it everywhere, just as before, and so six times.”

Moreover, many lotus flowers of treasure fill the whole world. Each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand kotis of petals. Their light is immeasurable; the colors are countless. Blue hues emit blue light, white hues emit white light; dark, yellow, coral, and purple, their light and color likewise. There are also immeasurable superb treasures, a hundred thousand mani gems, adorning the rare and wondrous, shining upon sun and moon.

“The size of those lotuses is either half a yojana, or one, two, three, four, up to a hundred thousand yojanas. From each flower there issue thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of rays of light. Within each ray there appear thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of Buddhas, their bodies purple-gold, their marks and excellences surpassing and rare. Each of these Buddhas again emits a hundred thousand rays of light, and universally for the ten directions speaks the subtle Dharma. Such Buddhas each establish immeasurable beings upon the Buddha’s right Way.”

All those reborn in the worlds of the ten directions are spontaneously born by transformation within the lotus flowers of the seven-jeweled pools. They all receive a pure, ethereal body, a body without limit. They never hear the names of the three evil paths’ evil afflictions and miseries. If those names do not even exist, how much less the actual suffering? There is only the sound of natural happiness. Therefore that land is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

blocks.text: 22. Dwelling in the Stage of Rightness

inline.s: Moreover, Ananda, that Buddha-land has no darkness, no fire-light, no sun, moon, or stars
yào

, no appearance of day or night, no name of months, years, or kalpas, and no attachment to homes and families. In every place, having neither markers nor names, neither grasping nor rejecting nor discriminating, they receive only purity and the utmost happiness.

If good men or good women, whether already born or to be born there, all dwell in the stage of rightness, they will certainly realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Why? Because those in the stage of wrongness and the undecided stage cannot understand the causes that establish that stage.

blocks.text: 23. Praises of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions

inline.s: Moreover, Ananda, in the worlds of the East as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in each of these worlds, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges each put forth the broad and long tongue, emit immeasurable light, and speak truthful words, praising the inconceivable merits of Amitabha Buddha. The Buddhas of the South, West, and North, in Ganges-sand worlds, praise him likewise. In the four intermediate quarters, above and below, in Ganges-sand worlds, the Buddhas praise him likewise.

Why is this? Because they wish all beings of other lands, hearing that Buddha’s name, to give rise to a pure mind, recollect, receive, and uphold it, and take refuge and make offerings. Even those able to give rise to a single thought of pure faith, with all their good roots, sincerely dedicating them, wishing to be born in that land—according to their vows they shall all be born there, never regressing, up to supreme right enlightenment.
The Buddha told Ananda: “In the worlds of the ten directions, among the gods and humans, those who with sincere heart wish to be born in that land fall into three grades.”

“The highest grade are those who, abandoning home and desire, become sramanas, give rise to the bodhi mind, singly and constantly recollect Amitabha Buddha, cultivate all merits, and wish to be born in that land. Such beings, at the end of their lives, have Amitabha Buddha and the great assembly appear before them, and then follow that Buddha to be born in his land. In the lotus flower of the seven-jeweled pool they are spontaneously born by transformation, abiding in non-regression, with wisdom brave and keen, supernormal powers free and spontaneous. Therefore, Ananda, beings who wish to see Amitabha Buddha in this life should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi, cultivate merit and virtue, and wish to be born in that land.”

“The middle grade are those who, though unable to practice as sramanas or greatly cultivate merits, should give rise to the bodhi mind, singly and constantly recollect Amitabha Buddha, and cultivate some good. They observe the fasts and precepts, raise stupas and images, provide meals for sramanas, hang streamers and light lamps, scatter flowers and burn incense, and with this dedicate the merit, wishing to be born in that land. At death Amitabha Buddha transforms a body, with light and marks completely like the true Buddha, and with the great assembly appears before them. They follow the transformed Buddha and are born in his land, abiding in non-regression; their merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the highest grade.”

“The lowest grade are those who, even if unable to do all the merits, should give rise to the bodhi mind, singly and constantly recollect Amitabha Buddha, up to ten recollections, wishing to be born in his land. And there are beings who, hearing the profound Dharma, rejoice in faith and delight, without doubt, and even with a single thought recollect that Buddha, with a most sincere heart, wishing to be born in his land. At death they see Amitabha Buddha in a dream, and are also able to be reborn there; their merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.”

Moreover, Ananda, if a good man or good woman hears this scripture, receives, upholds, recites, copies, and makes offerings to it, continuing day and night, seeking birth in that land; gives rise to the bodhi mind, upholds all the precepts, firmly keeping them without violation; benefits sentient beings, and gives to them all the good roots he has done to bring them peace and joy; recollects Amitabha Buddha and his land—such a person, at the end of life, with the Buddha’s form and marks and all manner of adornment, is born in the jeweled land, quickly hears the Dharma, and never regresses.

Moreover, Ananda, if beings wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly practice vigor and meditation or fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should do good. That is: first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not sexual misconduct; fourth, not false speech; fifth, not idle talk; sixth, not harsh speech; seventh, not slander; eighth, not greed; ninth, not anger; tenth, not foolishness. Thus day and night reflecting upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitabha Buddha’s manifold merits and manifold adornments, with a sincere heart take refuge, bow, and make offerings. Such a person, at death, without fright or fear, with mind not inverted, is then born in that Buddha-land.”

If one is occupied with many affairs and cannot leave home, and has not the leisure to greatly observe the fasts and precepts and keep a single mind pure, then, when he has spare time, let him rectify body and mind, abandon desire and put away sorrow, and with a loving heart be vigorous. He should not be angry or envious, nor gluttonous
(tiè)
or stingy
(qiān)
. He must not later regret, nor harbor doubt.

“He should be filial, sincere, and true. He should believe that the words of the Buddhist scriptures are profound, and that doing good brings blessings. He should uphold such teachings and not fail in them. Thinking and pondering deeply, wishing to attain liberation, day and night constantly recollecting, wishing to be reborn in Amitabha Buddha’s pure Buddha-land—those who for ten days and ten nights, or even one day and one night, do not break off, at death shall all be reborn in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.”

All those reborn there attain irreversibility, possess the true golden-colored body with thirty-two marks, and shall all become Buddhas. In whatever Buddha-land they wish to become a Buddha, it follows the wishes of their mind. According to their vigor, seeking the Way morning and evening without rest, they shall surely obtain it, without failing their vows.
Ananda, because of the benefit and advantage of this, in immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, incomparable, boundless worlds, all the Tathagatas together praise all the merits of Amitabha Buddha.

blocks.text: 26. Paying Homage to the Land of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: Moreover, Ananda, the hosts of bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to pay homage to Amitabha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, each with incense, flowers, banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies, go to that Buddha’s abode. They respectfully make offerings, hear and receive the Dharma, proclaim the Way and its transformation, and praise the adorning merits of that Buddha-land.
At that moment the World-Honored One spoke a verse:
The Buddha-lands of the East, numberless as the Ganges’ sands; hosts of bodhisattvas, like Ganges sands, go to pay homage to Immeasurable Life.
South, West, North, the four angles, above and below, likewise; all with a reverent heart offer precious and wondrous gifts.
They pour forth harmonious and elegant tones, singing the praises of the most supreme and honored One, penetrating to his transcendental wisdom, entering his deep Dharma-gate.
Hearing the name of the Buddha’s holy virtue, they gain peace and great advantage; among all manner of offerings, they diligently cultivate without slack or weariness.

Beholding that supremely wondrous land, subtle and beyond thought, its merits universally adorn it, no Buddha-land can compare; thereupon they raise the unsurpassed mind, and wish quickly to accomplish bodhi.

At that the Measureless Honored One smiled, and showed his golden face. Light issued from his mouth, universally illuminating the lands of the ten directions; the light returned and circled the Buddha, then entered his crown, making three rounds.
The bodhisattvas seeing this light straightway attained the stage of non-regression; all the assembly at that time rejoiced with one another.
The Buddha’s voice thundered like the Brahma bell, and with the eight tones he uttered the wondrous sound:
“The right-minded ones come from the ten directions; I know all their vows—they seek to adorn the pure land, and are to be predicted to become Buddhas.
Realizing all dharmas as like dream, illusion, and echo, they fulfill all the wondrous vows, and shall surely accomplish such a land.”

“Knowing the land as like a shadow or image, they ever raise the heart of great vows; they carry the bodhisattva path to perfection, complete the root of all merit, cultivate the supreme bodhi-conduct, and are to be predicted to become Buddhas.”
